todays_goal: Write with real revision, advance math to the coordinate plane, hold French futur proche to mastery, apply reflection in an engineering challenge, finish TacticLab motion/corner playback, deepen Hellenistic history, and repair point-of-view reasoning.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.previous_learning: Day 21 had the right Jalen/Mira contrast but did not fully meet the prompt; the self-edit named an awkward sentence without actually replacing it.
lessons.course_context: Writing remains the daily review subject. Require planning, exact evidence, outcome reasoning, and visible revision.
learning_objectives: Use one similarity and two differences
Explain why a difference changes the outcome
Replace a weak sentence with a stronger one
lessons.why_it_matters: Strong writing is built through planning, drafting, rereading, and real revision.

vocabulary.definition: a change that improves meaning, clarity, accuracy, or completeness
an exact detail that supports a claim

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: plan first, draft second, revise third. A revision is not naming a weak sentence; it is replacing that sentence with a stronger one.

worked_examples.title: Real revision
worked_examples.solution: Both teams want to release a working app.
worked_examples.explanation: The revision replaces vague words with the actual idea.

guided_practice.prompt: Fill the five-box comparison plan before drafting.

independent_practice.prompt: Write 8-9 sentences comparing Team Nova and Team Orbit with one similarity, two differences, evidence for both teams, and why one difference changes the outcome.
Complete the revision check and visibly replace one weak sentence.

exit_ticket.prompt: Score the draft using the strict 10-point gate and identify the sentence you truly improved.

lessons.voice_prompt: Be strict and concise. Require the five-box plan before drafting. During revision, have Atticus read the weak sentence aloud, explain what is wrong, and rewrite it himself. Do not dictate the assigned paragraph.
lessons.teacher_notes: Revision points require an actual changed sentence.

lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.previous_learning: Day 21 inequalities were strong; equation versus inequality definition still needs brief retrieval.
lessons.course_context: Move into plotting and reading ordered pairs across all four quadrants.
lessons.why_it_matters: Coordinate planes connect number lines to graphing, geometry, and data.

vocabulary.definition: two numbers written (x, y) that locate a point

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: ordered pairs are x first, y second. Move left/right for x, then up/down for y.

independent_practice.prompt: Write the ordered pair for 3 right and 5 down.

exit_ticket.prompt: What does the first number in an ordered pair tell you?
Write the coordinate for 6 right and 2 down.

lessons.voice_prompt: Use the whiteboard coordinate plane. Repeat x first, then y. Ask Atticus to say the sign pattern before naming a quadrant. Use different points from the assigned work.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.previous_learning: Day 21 still included vous allez regardez for they are going to watch and tu/elle form errors.
lessons.course_context: One final focused mastery gate before adding new grammar.
lessons.why_it_matters: Automatic subject-verb matching frees attention for meaning.

vocabulary.definition: aller plus an infinitive to say what someone is going to do

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: subject + correct ALLER + infinitive. Ils vont regarder. Tu vas lire. Elle va manger.

worked_examples.title: Three-part check
worked_examples.explanation: Check subject, aller form, then infinitive.

independent_practice.prompt: Translate: They are going to watch the match.
Translate: You are going to read. (tu)
Translate: She is going to eat.
Translate: We are going to play.

exit_ticket.prompt: Say six futur proche sentences without looking.
exit_ticket.answer: 6/6 written and at least 5/6 oral to advance.

lessons.voice_prompt: Oral first. Make Atticus say subject, aller form, and infinitive before the full sentence. If wrong, identify only the wrong component. Do not give the whole assigned answer.
lessons.teacher_notes: If gate fails, continue brief retrieval next day.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.previous_learning: Day 21 showed solid virtual-image understanding; the ray model used only one reflected ray instead of the requested two-ray construction.
lessons.course_context: Apply the law of reflection in a two-mirror design challenge.
learning_objectives: Apply angle in equals angle out
Explain how mirror angle redirects light
lessons.why_it_matters: Engineering applies predictable science rules to achieve a target outcome.

vocabulary.definition: a condition the solution must satisfy

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: use two mirrors to redirect light from a source to a target. At each mirror, angle in must equal angle out from the normal.

worked_examples.title: Around a corner
worked_examples.problem: Send light to a target that is not in a straight line.
worked_examples.explanation: Each mirror angle directs the next ray.

independent_practice.prompt: Draw source, target, two mirrors, normals, and reflected rays.
Explain how your mirrors redirect the light.

exit_ticket.prompt: Why can changing a mirror's angle change where reflected light goes?
exit_ticket.answer: It changes the normal and reflected direction.

exit_ticket.prompt: What rule must be true at each mirror?
exit_ticket.answer: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.

lessons.voice_prompt: Use the whiteboard as an engineering diagram. Make Atticus place mirror 1 first, predict the outgoing ray, then place mirror 2. Ask for the normal at each reflection. Do not draw his finished assigned design.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.unit_title: Creative Technology and AI Builder Lab
lessons.previous_learning: Core coaching controls passed on Day 20. Day 21 assigned animated tactic playback and a corner routine, but no finished build evidence was submitted.
lessons.course_context: Resume the same build and require a working demo before any new feature.
lessons.why_it_matters: Builders finish and verify core behavior instead of abandoning nearly complete features.

vocabulary.definition: whether animation is playing, paused, stopped, or reset
run the same test again after a fix

lessons.written_instruction: Laptop only. Finish PLAY, PAUSE/STOP, RESET, formation-safe playback, and the replayable corner routine. No new feature until those pass.

worked_examples.title: Bug report
worked_examples.problem: Reset returns players to the wrong formation.
worked_examples.explanation: A precise report proves whether state logic really works.

guided_practice.prompt: Put the current failing acceptance test on the whiteboard.

independent_practice.prompt: Verify PLAY.
Verify PAUSE/STOP and RESET.
Verify formation switching.
Finish and replay the corner routine twice.

exit_ticket.prompt: Demo play, pause/stop, reset, formation change, and corner routine twice. Explain the hardest bug and retest.

lessons.voice_prompt: Laptop only. Keep only the current failing acceptance test plus EXPECTED / ACTUAL / STEPS / RETEST on the whiteboard. Do not allow a new feature until the current test passes.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.previous_learning: Day 21 showed strong understanding of Alexandria as a center of trade, learning, and cultural exchange.
lessons.course_context: Use Euclid, Eratosthenes, and Archimedes to show Hellenistic mathematics, science, and engineering.
learning_objectives: Connect Archimedes with math and engineering
lessons.why_it_matters: Connected societies can accelerate knowledge through observation, mathematics, and exchange.

vocabulary.definition: study of shapes, space, and relationships
distance around a circle or sphere

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: focus on what each thinker did and HOW reasoning or mathematics helped them reach conclusions.

worked_examples.title: Eratosthenes
worked_examples.problem: How could shadows help estimate Earth's size?
worked_examples.explanation: A local measurement can be scaled into a huge estimate.

independent_practice.prompt: What subject is Euclid linked with?
What did Eratosthenes estimate?
What kind of work made Archimedes famous?

exit_ticket.prompt: Choose one thinker and explain what he did, how he used reasoning or mathematics, and why it mattered in 4 sentences.

lessons.voice_prompt: Use three columns: EUCLID / ERATOSTHENES / ARCHIMEDES. Add one main contribution under each. For Eratosthenes, draw a simple two-city shadow diagram. Keep explanations concrete.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.lesson_title: Point of View Repair: The Weather Call
lessons.previous_learning: Day 21 correctly identified Niko's extra information and that the missed result did not automatically make the pass bad, but one POV question was blank and the theme was vague.
lessons.course_context: Short targeted review separating information available at the time from later outcome.
learning_objectives: Explain different judgments of the same event
lessons.why_it_matters: Good reasoning judges decisions using information available at the time rather than only the result.

vocabulary.definition: what a character knows or can observe when deciding

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: do not confuse the result with the quality of the decision. Ask what each person knew at the time.

worked_examples.title: Decision vs result
worked_examples.problem: A good pass leads to a missed shot.
worked_examples.solution: The miss does not automatically make the pass bad.
worked_examples.explanation: Judge the choice using information available at the time.

independent_practice.prompt: Why is Jordan annoyed at first?
What information does Coach Lena have?
Does bright sky prove the cancellation was bad?
What changes Jordan's point of view?

exit_ticket.prompt: In 3 sentences, explain why Jordan and Coach Lena judge the cancellation differently at first. Use one exact detail.
exit_ticket.answer: Contrast their information and use the radar or bright-sky detail.

lessons.voice_prompt: Keep wording simple. Ask what each person knew at that moment. If Atticus judges only from the later outcome, ask whether that information was available when the decision was made. Require one exact detail.
lessons.teacher_notes: Short repair after mostly successful Day 21 POV work.
